Tor stalled at %1$d%% and couldn\'t reach the Tor network. This is exactly what a Tor-filtering network produces. Turn on bridges in Settings → Tor, or use Aether → Tor mode: there, Tor is built from inside the tunnel and the operator can neither see nor block it.
The engine ran but Tor reported no progress toward the Tor network. Make sure the internet is working, then try Aether → Tor mode, which builds Tor inside the tunnel.
Tor reached the network but no connection opened from inside it. Try again — and if it repeats, use Aether → Tor mode.
Tor couldn\'t reach the Tor network in time. On a network that blocks Tor, use Aether → Tor mode: the connection is built inside the tunnel there and can\'t be blocked.

Tor alone, without the Aether tunnel. Your exit is a Tor exit node and traffic passes through three relays: the slowest and most private mode. Here Tor has to reach the Tor network itself, so it uses a bridge if blocked.

Two hops: Aether connects first, then Tor is built inside that same tunnel. The network you\'re on only ever sees Aether\'s obfuscated transport, never Tor — so wherever Tor is blocked, pick this mode. Your exit is a Tor exit node.

Three hops: Tor first, then Psiphon from inside it. Your exit IP is Psiphon\'s, reached from a Tor address; so sites that block Tor exit nodes open, and your own address stays behind Tor. The slowest mode.
Tor picks its own exit node, a fresh one for every circuit. No setting restricts it to one country.
How to reach the network when Tor is blocked.
Not needed in this mode: Tor connects from inside the Aether tunnel, so the network you\'re on never sees it.
One per line, in the format bridges.torproject.org gives you. Leave empty and the app fetches bridges for your country itself. A line naming a transport the app doesn\'t ship is ignored.

Tor carries TCP only — in every app, on every platform. Aether resolves DNS over TCP inside Tor and drops the rest of the UDP, so apps that use QUIC fall back to TCP. That\'s normal and nothing leaks: dropped UDP goes nowhere, let alone around Tor. Expect noticeably more latency, and expect the first connection to take a while — Tor downloads its directory before building a circuit.

The reverse chain: Tor first, then the Aether tunnel is built inside it. Your exit is a WARP address — the same thing plain Aether gives — but the network you\'re on only sees Tor and can\'t tell a VPN tunnel exists at all. Useful where Cloudflare/WARP itself is blocked or throttled but Tor still gets through. Unlike the Tor-exit modes, it carries normal UDP.
This mode is locked to MASQUE over HTTP/2. Tor carries TCP only, and WARP\'s WireGuard endpoints answer on UDP alone, so the engine won\'t accept WireGuard or WARP×2 here.
Which country\'s bridges bridgedb should give. Auto-detect asks the network where you are, and that very request is the one most likely to fail here.
How long Tor tries the direct path before turning to bridges. Shorten it if you\'re sure Tor is blocked.
The address Tor must reach for bootstrap to count as successful. Only change it if bootstrap keeps failing while Tor looks healthy — the default target itself is blocked on some networks.
